paras: The lynching of James P. Holland was the hanging of a prisoner accused of murder by masked men who broke into the jail at Dardanelle, Yell County, Arkansas, about midnight on November 26–27, 1881. Holland had escaped jail before a verdict in his trial for an 1879 killing and had been returned from Tennessee hours earlier; he was hanged in the jail yard where a mob had hanged a man named Taylor months before. Papers nationwide carried it as another Arkansas lynching, while a Russellville paper printed a letter defending it.

According to a Little Rock special, Holland conspired in 1879 with William Casey and Charles G. Helphrey to rob Burgess James, and Helphrey shot him on the bank of the Arkansas River. The dead man was a "young and eccentric planter" in that report, an old cotton picker in a Dardanelle dispatch, and "an old negro" in the Lexington (Mo.) Weekly Intelligencer; several wire reports called him Burgess Jones.

Casey was twice sentenced to hang; Holland's trial at Ozark ended, a Russellville correspondent wrote, in a hung jury. A jail guard named Hill, said to have been bribed or brought from Tennessee by Holland's uncle, later let the three men out. In November Sheriff J. C. Hannah of Polk County, Tennessee, arrested Holland, recognizing him from a picture sent from Arkansas.

According to the Dardanelle dispatch, Hannah, expecting trouble, left the train at Russellville for a private conveyance, and about twenty-five armed, masked men stopped the train farther on and searched it for Holland. The Dardanelle Post said Holland reached the jail about six that evening.

Accounts of the entry about midnight differ: the Chicago Tribune's Little Rock special said about fifty men came and the jailer and guards surrendered without a blow, while the Dardanelle dispatch said the jailer refused the keys and the door was broken with sledge hammers. The Post said the guards, Lee Smith and Charley Hearn, were asleep when raiders with cocked pistols took their keys and struck Smith with a pistol barrel.

In the Tribune's version Holland, handcuffed, was told the men wanted "Your life" and was quickly overpowered. The dispatch recorded his last words, a plea for mercy on his wife and children, cut off when he was gagged. He was hanged in the jail yard from the beam, "scantling" or tree used for Taylor, and the men crossed the river toward Russellville, the Tribune said.

The body hung in the jail yard until noon Sunday awaiting the coroner, while crowds gathered at the jail. The coroner's inquest returned "the usual findings," death at the hands of unknown parties, and the body went to friends. No arrest of any mob member was reported, though Hill, the guard who had freed the prisoners, was said to be arrested.

The Russellville Democrat denied the Dardanelle Arkansian's implication that the mob came from Pope County by the ferry. Wire reports called it the county's third lynching in a year, and the Russellville letter named Bruce and Taylor as earlier victims.

The Chicago Tribune headed its report "Another Victim of a Maddened Mob of Lynchers in Arkansas" and said the lynching had "disgraced" the county. The Dardanelle dispatch, carried by the Memphis Appeal, the Press and Daily Dakotaian and the Cleveland (Tenn.) Weekly Herald, called it "another disgraceful tragedy" but detailed Holland's confession. One-line items ran from St. Paul to Gold Hill and Dallas, some with the name garbled as "James Howard" or "Holcomb."

The Russellville Democrat reprinted the Post's headline, "Returned to his Friends, Who Received Him with an Open Rope," and a letter signed "Z." concluding that "mob justice is better than no justice." The Osceola Times joked that "Guiteau and other cranks should be sent to Dardanelle." The Eaton (Ohio) Democrat alone questioned Holland's guilt, noting that he confessed only to knowing of the crime.

Local accounts place the hanging between midnight Saturday and early Sunday, November 27; the St. Paul Globe said Saturday night and the Dallas Herald Monday morning. Accounts of Holland's role differed: the Tribune said he laid the plot, the Dardanelle dispatch that he confessed to instigating it, and the Eaton Democrat that he only knew of it.

reader.title: Lynching of James P. Holland
bases: A band of masked men broke into the Dardanelle jail and hanged a prisoner held on a murder charge (A5, A6, A11).

Holland was taken from the jail by a mob of twenty-five to fifty men and hanged with no legal authority (A5, A8, A29); the papers tie the act to his accused part in an 1879 murder and his escape from punishment, and a local letter defended it as 'justice' (A4, A12).
The Chicago Tribune's Little Rock special, a separate Dardanelle dispatch, and the local Dardanelle Post and Russellville letter all report the jail break and hanging (A5, A6, A11, A10).

accounts.gist: About fifty men surrounded the jail at 1 a.m., the jailer and guards surrendered without a blow, and Holland, handcuffed, was overpowered and hanged over a beam in the jail yard; the mob crossed the river toward Russellville.

accounts.label: Dardanelle dispatch (Nov. 28)
accounts.gist: About twenty-five masked men stopped the train beyond Russellville looking for Holland, then reached Dardanelle at midnight, broke the jail door with sledge hammers after the jailer refused the keys, gagged Holland and hanged him from Taylor's tree.

accounts.label: Dardanelle Post, local
accounts.gist: Holland arrived about six Saturday evening; the jail was broken open at 12 by unknown parties; the guards were asleep and the raiders with cocked pistols took their keys; the coroner's inquest found 'unknown parties'.

framing.detail: Chicago Tribune: headline 'Another Victim of a Maddened Mob of Lynchers in Arkansas'; the third lynching that 'disgraced' the county.
Dardanelle dispatch calls it 'another disgraceful tragedy' but recounts Holland's confession and calls him 'the poor wretch'.
Russellville Democrat letter 'Z.': Yell County concluded 'mob justice is better than no justice'; the Post headline 'Returned to his Friends, Who Received Him with an Open Rope'.
Osceola Times treats it as a joke: 'Guiteau and other cranks should be sent to Dardanelle.'
Eaton Democrat: vengeance in Arkansas 'a little too summary' for those whose guilt is in doubt.
One-line news-summary briefs in St. Paul, Lancaster, Gold Hill, Dallas, Lexington and Grayling papers, several with garbled names.
